headline: Garment worker protests threaten Bangladesh's fragile economic recovery as hundreds of factories close
summary: Ongoing wage protests by garment workers have forced hundreds of factories to close, coinciding with mixed economic data indicating a slow and uneven national recovery.
details: Wage protests by garment workers entered their fourth day yesterday, leading to the closure of several hundred factories. This widespread unrest coincides with fresh economic data pointing to a fragile and uneven national recovery.

In the first four months of the fiscal year, exports grew by 6 percent and remittances by 13 percent. However, mounting import payment pressure is pushing the Taka lower against the dollar, with imports rising by 12 percent in July-August.

Private sector credit growth fell to a record low of 4.17 percent in September, signaling continued weakness in investment and business activity. Inflation remains stubbornly high, staying close to 8.5 percent.

Economists warn that prolonged unrest in the garment sector could disrupt production and exports, negatively impacting the overall economy. They emphasize that the economy has yet to show a meaningful turnaround.

Mustafizur Rahman of the Centre for Policy Dialogue stated that slow growth, weak investment, and persistent inflation continue to weigh on economic activity. He noted that export growth of around 6 percent fell short of the double-digit target.

Ashikur Rahman, principal economist at the Policy Research Institute of Bangladesh, highlighted the alarmingly low private sector credit growth. He explained that with credit growing slower than inflation, it is contracting in real terms, indicating weak demand for investment loans and constraints on banks’ ability to lend.

Experts stress that credible dialogue addressing workers’ wage and cost-of-living concerns is essential to protect livelihoods and export competitiveness. Stabilisation measures and critical reforms are also needed to revive economic growth while bringing inflation under control.

Recommendations include ensuring a steady improvement in foreign exchange reserves, gradually reducing inflation, tackling non-performing loans in the banking sector, and improving revenue collection. Ensuring uninterrupted power and gas supplies to export-oriented industries is also crucial.

headline_marked: [[Millions cast ballots in US midterms]] as polls close, control of Congress hangs in balance
headline: Millions cast ballots in US midterms as polls close, control of Congress hangs in balance
summary: Americans are voting to decide whether Republicans will retain control of Congress. Exit polls show widespread dissatisfaction, with many voters aiming to rebuke President Trump.
details: Polls have closed in several US states as millions of Americans cast their ballots in the midterm elections. Voters are determining whether to strip control of Congress from President Trump's Republicans, with Democrats favored to capture the House.

The fate of both the House and Senate may not be known for some time as election workers tally ballots. Historically, the sitting president's party tends to lose ground in Congress during midterms, a trend that works against Republicans.

Exit polls indicate that half of voters view these elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president. Three-quarters of those surveyed expressed anger or dissatisfaction with the country's direction, and 70% want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

President Trump has actively campaigned, urging supporters to "pretend I'm on the ballot." He also made televised remarks on Tuesday, appearing to sway voters unhappy with US support for Israel by stating his intention to stop annual funding.

Republicans, led by Trump, have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, while Democrats dismiss these labels as hyperbole. Voter concerns are primarily focused on affordability, an issue on which Trump's handling has drawn disapproval.

Legal observers and Democrats have raised concerns that Trump might challenge the results if Republicans lose, citing his past false claims of rigged elections. In response, the US Justice Department deployed 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states, the largest monitoring effort in history.

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate's 100 seats are up for election. Democrats need to flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to secure a majority in each chamber.

There are 47 US House races considered competitive, and Democrats would need to win just 13 of these to gain a majority if other contests proceed as predicted. The Senate race is tighter, requiring Democrats to defend current seats and win at least two states that strongly voted for Trump in 2024.
